prompt: Which of these recurrences solve to **Θ(log n)**, growing like the logarithm of n? T(n) is the running time on input size n. Select all that apply.

options.text: One half-size call plus constant work
options.explanation: Yes. One half-size subproblem with constant outside work has logarithmic depth: binary-search growth.

options.text: One third-size call plus constant work
options.explanation: Yes. Changing the fixed divisor changes the logarithm base but only by a constant factor.

options.text: One call one item smaller, plus constant work
options.explanation:
No. Subtracting 1 takes n steps to reach the base case, so this is Θ(n).

Here n is the current subproblem size.

options.text: Two half-size calls plus constant work
options.explanation:
No. Two subproblems per level means the number of nodes doubles each level; the n leaves dominate, giving Θ(n).

Here n is the current subproblem size.

options.text: One half-size call plus logarithmic work
options.explanation: No. A logarithmic contribution on each shrinking level accumulates to the square of a logarithm.

workedExample: One fixed-fraction child with constant outside work gives one constant contribution per level and logarithmic depth. Subtracting one instead gives linear depth. Two half-size children create a linear number of nodes. One halving child with logarithmic outside work adds a descending sequence of logarithms, giving the square of a logarithm.

prompt: A recursion tree has two half-size children per node and outside work proportional to each node’s input size. Leaves have constant positive cost. Why is total work linear times logarithmic in original input size?

options.text: Only the leaf level does any work
options.explanation: Internal nodes also perform their own scans or merges.

options.text: The number of nodes equals the square of input size
options.explanation: The tree has a linear number of nodes; per-node work varies by level.

options.text: Each level contributes linear total work across logarithmically many levels
options.explanation: Correct. Branching doubles the nodes while halving their sizes, preserving each level’s total.

options.text: The root is always the only contribution that matters
options.explanation: Here later levels collectively add a logarithmic factor.

workedExample: Two half-size children preserve their parent’s total size. That repeats across each complete level until size-one leaves. Repeated halving gives logarithmic depth, so adding equal linear level totals introduces the logarithm. Base-case leaves matter for exact counts even though they add only a linear term.
